verdicts.trueWording: 76% of Total Fabrications layer semantic plausibility on wholesale invention
verdicts.note: arxiv.org/html/2602.05930 reached raw (abs + full HTML). Sec. text: 'among the 66 Total Fabrications, 50 cases (76%) utilized Semantic Hallucination as their secondary mode' and 'The fact that 76% of Total Fabrications specifically layer semantic plausibility on top of wholesale invention'. Abstract: 'every hallucination (100%) exhibited compound failure modes'. Both limbs supported. Graded SUBSTANCE only because the claim carries no quote field to match word-for-word; the page wording is near-identical. Caution: the abstract's ALL-citation secondary-mode figure is 63%, a different denominator from the claim's 76%-of-TF.

verdicts.trueWording: a group of 24 drivers ... had actually taken a detour
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'coach parties' - the article reports one group of 24 DRIVERS on a trip from the mainland, not coach/bus parties
verdicts.note: euronews.com raw article fetched (browser UA). Quote verbatim: 'I said, ‘If you find the hot springs, come back and let me know and I’ll shout you beers all night’. They didn’t come back.' Supported: 'the (non-existent) Weldborough Hot Springs is listed alongside the (real) Hastings Caves and Thermal Springs'; 'complete with AI-generated images'; 'Weldborough, however, has never had hot springs'; posted July, 'a steady stream of duped travellers' to a Jan-2026 piece = months. Only the vehicle/party type is wrong.

verdicts.trueWording: paid about €140 to reach a remote rural road without a destination
verdicts.note: Same Euronews raw page. 'two tourists in Peru set off to find the “Sacred Canyon of Humantay” in the Andes Mountains – before a local tour guide overheard them and stopped them... They had reportedly paid about €140 to reach a remote rural road “without a guide or [a destination]”'; and 'two travellers used ChatGPT to plan a romantic sunset hike up a mountain in Japan... the AI tool had given them incorrect operating hours for the ropeway to get down and they were stuck in the dark.' Both limbs supported. SUBSTANCE not VERBATIM because the claim supplies no quote. Note the article attributes both cases to earlier BBC reporting.

verdicts.trueWording: towns by the names of “Orangeotild” and “Whata Bod” ... wild hallucinations of AI
verdicts.note: vice.com raw article fetched. 'Whata Bod' appears word for word. 'the Weather Service confirmed the graphic was created using generative AI, which had hallucinated entire communities and gave them appropriately silly names.' Idaho NWS wind-forecast map confirmed. (Aside: Vice's own text says 'Ohio residents' - an error in the source, not in the claim; the map and headline are Idaho.)

verdicts.trueWording: AI tools fabricate citations. They invent record collections.
verdicts.note: denyseallen.substack.com raw page fetched. Exact sentence: 'AI tools fabricate citations. They invent record collections. They create plausible-sounding sources that don’t exist.' Quote 'They invent record collections.' matches word for word; both limbs supported. The claim's 'whole' is an added intensifier with no counterpart on the page, and 'that do not exist' attaches on the page to 'sources', not to the collections - neither changes the substance.

verdicts.trueWording: AI will present fabricated sources, invented dates, and fictional ancestors with total confidence.
verdicts.note: Same raw Substack page. Quote 'fictional ancestors with total confidence' appears word for word inside that sentence; every limb (fabricated sources, invented dates, fictional ancestors, total confidence) is present.

verdicts.trueWording: agents tasked with “filling in gaps” can create plausible fake records
verdicts.note: Same raw Substack page: 'AI agents tasked with “filling in gaps” can create plausible fake records. A fabricated marriage record. An invented census entry. A person who never existed.' All three examples present. Claim carries no quote, so SUBSTANCE. Modality flag: the source states this as a forward-looking platform risk ('can create'), not as an observed incident; the claim's flat present tense reads as a disposition, which is what the page asserts.

verdicts.trueWording: human summaries beat out their AI competitors on every criteria and on every submission
verdicts.note: Live crikey.com.au is paywalled after four paragraphs; recovered the full text from the Wayback raw capture 20240903043403id_. Quote 'might actually create additional work for people' verbatim in the lede. 'five submissions from a parliamentary inquiry into audit and consultancy firms' for ASIC; reviewers 'found that the human summaries beat out their AI competitors on every criteria and on every submission, scoring an 81% on an internal rubric compared with the machine’s 47%'; reviewers said AI summaries 'may be counterproductive and create further work'. Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: GPTZero is black-box; the second tool, Binoculars, is 'more transparent'
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'the detectors black-box' (plural) - only GPTZero is; the Signpost explicitly calls the second detector, the open-source Binoculars, 'more transparent'
verdicts.note: en.wikipedia.org raw wikitext (?action=raw) fetched. Quote 'concept drift' verbatim: 'The authors are clearly aware of this [[concept drift]] problem, but only make a very perfunctory attempt to address it'. Supported: 'both tools disagreed frequently, with GPTZero being much more detection-happy than Binoculars in English, French, and German, but much less in Italian'; 'the fact that additional edits by human Wikipedia editors make the AI detection score go up in both detectors might increase skepticism'. The black-box property is quoted from the paper about GPTZero alone.

verdicts.trueWording: I don't think this is a reliable indicator of human or AI writing
verdicts.note: Wikipedia talk raw wikitext fetched. Section '== Citations at the end of paragraphs ==' (proposed by Quxyz, 21 Aug 2026). Thryduulf: 'This is something that I've seen in articles for the whole of the two decades I've been reading Wikipedia... I don't think this is a reliable indicator of human or AI writing.' Bearcat concurs: 'human editors have been doing the same thing for decades.' Proposer stood down: 'Pretty much what I wanted to know before doing an in-depth hunt'. Quote 'not a reliable indicator' verbatim (twice). 'Rejected' is a fair reading of a talk-page consensus, not a formal delisting.

verdicts.trueWording: updating markdown section - LLMs aren't bad at wikitext to this extent anymore
verdicts.note: Revision-history page fetched raw with a browser UA. 20:09, 27 August 2026, Gnomingstuff, -84 bytes, summary 'updating markdown section - LLMs aren't bad at wikitext to this extent anymore -- and hopefully also condensing' (plus a -6 m edit at 20:10 to 'Use of Markdown'). 10:18, 19 August 2026, EmoryNB, +5,008: 'added a new indicator for "Vague expression of connection or association"'. 23:12, 20 August 2026, Superb Owl, +1,259: 'adding subsection on content biases as possible indicators, with recent example of pro-authoritarian content', section 'Pro-authoritarian bias'. All three dates and directions confirmed; 'dated snapshot' is the researcher's inference, which the history supports.

verdicts.trueWording: task-specific MGT ... more closely resemble their human-written text (HWT) references
verdicts.note: arxiv.org/html/2507.03373v1 fetched raw (557KB). Quote verbatim: 'These results show that detectors struggle with MGT in realistic generation scenarios'. Numbers: 'training-based detectors achieve an average accuracy of 78%, while zero-shot detectors average 58%' - the claim's 58-78% band. Resemblance limb: 'the textual characteristics of task-specific MGT—unlike open-ended, topic-to-text MGT—more closely resemble their human-written text (HWT) references.' The three tasks are Paragraph Writing, Summarisation (lead-section generation per the MoS) and Text Style Transfer (neutralisation, via mWNC/WNC) - so 'lead summarisation' and 'neutralisation' both check out.

verdicts.trueWording: most common undesired behavior ... hallucinating, or making up, facts about the monsters
verdicts.note: ar5iv full text fetched raw. Verbatim: 'The most common undesired behavior DMs noticed was the model hallucinating, or making up, facts about the monsters, such as giving giant spiders telepathy (P15), an insect monster a poison ability (P8), or a frost salamander wings (P14).' Quote 'giving giant spiders telepathy' matches word for word. 71 participants: 'invited 71 players and DMs (referred to as P1-71)'; Discord: 'All gameplay occurred on our Discord server.' Scope note (not a failed limb): that sentence sits in the Abstractive Understanding results paragraph, i.e. it is the most common complaint about that interface rather than an aggregate across all three.

verdicts.trueWording: simply rephrasing the information in the monster's reference material
verdicts.note: Same ar5iv raw text. Quote verbatim (curly apostrophe on page): 'DMs argued that simply rephrasing the information in the monster’s reference material “doesn’t really help in running an encounter” (P8)'. Model identity: 'we prompted GPT-3 (Brown et al. 2020) (specifically, the text-davinci-003 model)'. Stats limb: 'when prompted with the task to summarize provided information, GPT-3 would focus too much on numeric game stats (despite the prompt stating not to)' and 'the model’s output simply paraphrased the information written in the setting and stat block'. Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: the model would often include the phrase “mythology and common sense” verbatim in its output
verdicts.note: Same ar5iv raw text: 'We also found that if we repeated a certain phrase multiple times in the prompt, e.g. “you may use information from mythology and common sense” ..., the model would often include the phrase “mythology and common sense” verbatim in its output. This is likely a case of degenerative output (Holtzman et al. 2020). To prevent this, each time a set phrase would have been templated in, we instead randomly chose 2-4 words from the set {”folklore”, “common sense”, “mythology”, “culture”} and inserted them in a random order.' Quote matches word for word including the curly quotes; prompt phrase and the randomisation remedy both confirmed.
